a-jilted-bride-for-the-battle-scarred-du.heading: Prologue: The Last Ball
paras: “Miss Raye, I must inform you, upon reflection and with the counsel of my family, that our engagement can no longer proceed.”
What a loathsome popinjay.

The thought arrived before the disgust did, and the disgust arrived before Ariana noticed the spinach lodged in his teeth. A vicar’s daughter was meant to receive ruin with dignified composure, and ruin was what Lionel Lockhart, heir to Viscount Fenmore, was handing her in the middle of a ballroom with three hundred people watching.
“I beg your pardon?” she said, not because she had failed to hear him, but to make him repeat it to her face and watch him try.

“The disparity in our situations,” Lionel began, addressing a point roughly six inches to the left of her ear, “has been brought to my attention more fully. Your father’s debts, you understand, are not the sort of thing a family in my position can easily overlook. And so I find I must, with the greatest reluctance, withdraw.”
“My father’s debts,” Ariana repeated pleasantly. “Which you have known about since March.”
“Yes, well. The thing of it is, you must see how it looks.” He had the air of a man reciting a lesson. “A man in my position—”
“Knew about them when he proposed,” she finished for him. “Do go on. You were explaining how it looks.”
“Ariana, if you would only allow me to explain—”
“Which your mother knew about,” she went on, touching the seed-pearl bodice of her gown with one finger, lightly, as though testing whether it was still real, “when she sent me this dress.”

The dress had arrived in a box so enormous she had at first taken it for a writing desk. Ivory silk, smelling of a lady’s dressing room. She had accepted it because refusing would have been rude, and because some stubborn part of her had thought, just once, that she deserved one beautiful thing. A remarkably stupid thought, as it turned out.
“Tell me, my lord.” Her voice dropped, quiet in a way that made him take half a step backward. “Was the gown intended as a parting gift? Or merely the costume for this particular performance?”
He opened his mouth. He had rehearsed for a scene in which the other actor had no lines, and was discovering, to his alarm, that she did.
“Ariana—”
“Miss Raye,” she corrected, and the correction shut like a door.
“Miss Raye, please, you must understand. I did not want this. That is to say, I fought. Mother has been most insistent, and a man cannot always—”
“Oh, do stop stammering, Lionel. You are making a spectacle of yourself, and there is already quite enough spectacle to go round.”

“That is the difficulty.” The Viscountess Fenmore stepped forward as though the three square feet she occupied were the whole of the room. She was shorter than Ariana, and carried herself as though she stood a head taller and had never once in fifty-seven years entertained a doubt. “I trust you understand, Miss Raye, that this decision, painful as it is, serves everyone’s best interest. A connection between our family and a woman of your circumstances is not a thing we can countenance.”
“My circumstances.” Ariana tilted her head. “You mean a vicar’s daughter whose entire inheritance consists of a talent for Latin verbs and an intimate acquaintance with the price of tallow candles.”
“I was going to say background.” The Viscountess smiled, cold as a January sunrise. “But you have illustrated my point exactly.”
“Have I? How efficient of me.”

The sapphire ring on her left hand caught the candlelight and threw small blue sparks across the Viscountess’s turban. Lionel had given it to her with trembling fingers and a speech about destiny she now suspected he had cribbed from a novel. He had met her the summer before, at the wedding of a cousin whose living her father held, and had pursued her past every objection his mother raised, vowing that a vicar’s daughter with a clever tongue was worth a dozen heiresses, right up until the moment his mother proved otherwise. Whatever she did in the next thirty seconds would follow her into every drawing room in London for years. Her future had dropped clean through the floor, and her mind had gone strangely, cleanly calm.
Let us make it worth remembering, then.
“You are quite right, my lady,” Ariana said. “The disparity is unconscionable. Your son can scarcely conjugate in English. I ought to have aimed considerably higher.”

The Viscountess went the colour of old parchment. Beside her, Lionel made a small, strangled sound, as though he had arranged for two women he feared to collide and only now seen where he was standing.
“How dare you.” The Viscountess’s voice climbed. “How dare you speak to me so, you ungrateful little—”

“I dare quite easily. It is one of the few advantages of having nothing left to lose. You ought to try it sometime, my lady, though I daresay the sensation would be novel for a woman who has spent her whole life ensuring other people do the losing on her behalf.”

She turned to Lionel, whose handsome face was cycling through shock and guilt and something that might, with more courage behind it, have become admiration. She could not even manage to hate him. He was weak rather than cruel, and the distinction mattered to her, even if the result did not.
“You were going to toast me tonight,” she said, and her voice softened at the edges without her leave. “You said you would raise your glass to the cleverest woman in London.”
“Ariana, I never meant for any of this to happen. I swear it.”
“Don’t.” The softness vanished. “You do not get to be sorry and do this also. That is not how it works.”
The champagne in her hand had gone tepid and flat, its bubbles long since surrendered. She had been holding it twenty minutes, saving it for a toast that was never going to come.
If I am to be ruined, she decided, I may as well be spectacular about it.

She threw the champagne in his face. A flick of the wrist, years of practice pouring at a vicar’s table distilled into a single motion. It caught him squarely across the nose and mouth, and his Italian silk cravat was ruined.

The ballroom went silent all at once, three hundred people ceasing to speak in the same instant, so that Ariana could hear the champagne dripping from Lionel’s chin onto the parquet. The Viscountess’s mouth opened and closed without producing sound, which was, Ariana noted with vicious satisfaction, very likely a first.
She set the empty glass on the tray of a passing footman, who received it without expression.
“You will regret this,” the Viscountess said, very low, the words pitched for Ariana alone. “A girl in your position cannot afford an enemy of my consequence.”
“I find I cannot afford a great many things, my lady. Your friendship was never going to be among the ones I missed.”
“You insolent little baggage. You will not speak to me so, do you hear me—”
“Mother.” Lionel’s voice cracked across hers, and for one astonishing moment Ariana thought he might, at the very last, find his spine. “Mother, people are watching.”

“Let them,” Ariana said, before the Viscountess could answer. “I should hate to deprive them. It is the best entertainment Lady Castleton has provided all season, and the orchestra has not even resumed.”

She inclined her head to Lionel, who blinked champagne from his lashes like a man caught in an indoor rainstorm. “Thank you for a most illuminating evening, my lord. I have learned a great deal tonight about the character of the English aristocracy. On the whole, a most efficient education.”
She turned without curtsying, and the crowd parted before her, not out of deference but out of the perfectly reasonable fear that she might do it again. The whispers followed her like a draught.
“Did you see? She actually threw it. In his face.”
“The vicar’s girl. One always knew it would end badly. That sort never can hold a position above their station.”
“I thought it rather magnificent, personally,” murmured a third voice, a woman’s, older, somewhere near the card-room door. “He deserved every drop, and a good deal more than champagne.”
Behind her, the Viscountess said, in a voice that could have frozen the Thames in July, “Well. I trust that settles the matter.”

And Lionel, useless, beautiful, spineless Lionel, said nothing at all. That was the part that would hurt, Ariana understood as she collected her cloak. Not the words, nor the dress, nor the ring. His silence, when it had mattered most.

London slid past the carriage window, gaslight and shadow, indifferent to the small catastrophes of the people inside it. She did not weep until Berkeley Square. Then she wept with her fist pressed to her mouth, the raw, ragged breathing of a woman who had just burned her only bridge and could still smell the smoke.

She pulled the sapphire from her finger and dropped it into her cloak pocket, among the lint and a halfpenny and a folded receipt for candles. That was where things went when they stopped being precious.

“I will not be made small again,” she said aloud to the empty carriage, and her voice did not shake, which surprised her, because the rest of her was shaking badly. “Do you hear me? Not by him. Not by her. Not by any of them. Never again.”
The carriage gave no answer. It was, she reflected, the most agreeable conversation she had held all evening.

A softer woman might have sworn off love, or hope, or men. Ariana swore off smallness, and carried the vow up a narrow flight of stairs and into a narrow bed, and held it through the dawn and through everything the next two years saw fit to take from her.

When at last a road in Hampshire delivered her to a house full of silence and a man full of shadows, she still had it, bright and sharp as a blade. Whatever came next could not possibly be worse than a viscount’s heir wearing her champagne in front of three hundred people.
She was wrong about that. But she was not wrong about herself.

a-fiery-widow-for-the-cold-duke.heading: Chapter One
paras: There were two ways into the Duke of Wrenwick’s house, and Lord Nathaniel Harcourt had never in his life chosen the front, with its footman and its wait, when the side door yielded to nothing grander than a shoulder set against the place it always stuck. He had been opening that door since he was nine.
He arrived in the breakfast room before the clock had finished telling nine, road-dust on his boots and not a particle of shame about any of it.
“You look dreadful,” he said.

Alexander did not rise, nor turn his head, nor give the smallest sign that a man crossing forty miles of road to insult him before breakfast was an event worth interrupting a letter for. A duke learned young that the room would wait. He let it wait now, his attention on a page he was not in fact reading, until the silence had made his point for him.
“You entered my house before nine o’clock,” he said at last. “I had assumed we were abandoning courtesy on both sides, and I am relieved to have the matter confirmed so early in the day.”
“It is a wonder you have any servants left at all,” Harcourt said cheerfully, “the hours you keep them to.”

“I keep no particular hours,” Alexander replied evenly, setting down his pen at last. “The servants keep clear of me, which I have always taken for the natural order of things and you appear to take for a tragedy.”

“I take it for a symptom.” Harcourt drew out a chair across the vast expanse of the table and surveyed the spread upon it. He had ridden a long way without breakfast, and made no secret of his opinion of the oranges.

There were oranges that had travelled a very long way to reach a Surrey morning. There was chocolate, and good tea, and a fish that had no earthly business being so far from the sea, and a quantity of silver sufficient to ransom a minor prince. None of it had been touched, of course.
“Good God, Wrenwick. You have laid a table fit for the Regent himself and you sit here gnawing on a letter. Do you mean to eat any of this, or is it for decoration?”
“It is for the maintenance of standards.” Alexander set the letter down.

He had read it four times and could not have said what it contained, only that the hand was unfamiliar and the seal had been broken by someone other than himself, which in a house of this size meant nothing and unsettled him regardless.
“A duke’s table is laid every morning whether the duke chooses to dine or not. That is the difference between us, Harcourt. You are hungry. I am merely punctual.”

“You are merely stubborn, and you have dressed it in better tailoring than most men can afford for their virtues.” His friend laughed, which Alexander had not intended, and helped himself to one of the far-travelled oranges. “When did you last sit at this table with another living soul? And do not count me. I let myself in. I am less a guest than a draught.”
“I could not say,” Alexander answered, too quickly.
“No. That is rather my point.”

Behind them, at the sideboard, a footman whose name Alexander ought to have known gripped a coffee pot in both hands, frozen, braced against the moment he would be blamed for it. He had been standing so since Harcourt came in, as though stillness might render him invisible, and when Alexander turned his head at last the boy’s grip tightened and a thin dark trickle escaped the spout and crept across the polished wood.
“Leave it,” Alexander said, more sharply than the offence deserved.

The footman went the colour of the tablecloth and fled, abandoning the coffee to its fate. It was the general policy of the Wrenwick staff to flee first and tidy later, a system that kept the servants intact and the carpets considerably less so.
Harcourt watched him go. “You see, that is precisely what I have come about.”
“A footman who cannot pour?” Alexander said dryly.

“A house that flinches.” Harcourt peeled his orange with maddening unconcern, as though they were discussing the weather and not the thing that had taken up residence in Wrenwick Hall five years ago and never paid rent. “That boy is not clumsy. That boy is terrified, and terror has a way of travelling the back stairs faster than any order you ever gave. I have been in this house a quarter of an hour and I have met three servants and frightened all three merely by existing in their general direction. You have, what, thirty servants? Forty?”
“Thirty-two.”

It came out before he could weigh whether he wished to give it. The figure was always there, the way the count of horses in his stables was there, and the tally of tenants on his land, and the exact number of windows in the west wing that no longer opened. He carried such things without trying. What he could not have told anyone, this morning, was the last time he had eaten a full meal at his own table.

“Thirty-two,” Harcourt repeated, and the teasing had gone out of his voice, replaced by a gentleness Alexander liked even less. “Thirty-two souls under this roof, and you keep them all at such a careful distance that the house runs like a clock with sand in it. It is not that they do not work, Wrenwick. It is that they work afraid, and an estate run on fear is a slow estate, and you have run out of the one commodity a man in your position cannot purchase more of.”
“And what is that,” Alexander said, though he already knew.
“Time,” said Harcourt, gently.

Alexander leaned back. Outside the long windows the park lay grey and damp under a sky that had not decided whether to commit to rain, and the avenue of limes his grandfather had planted ran straight as a ruled line toward a gate he rarely troubled to pass through anymore.

“You have ridden from London at an hour fit for criminals to tell me my house is unhappy,” he said. “I am aware that my house is unhappy. I do not require a friend to inform me of it over my own oranges.”

“I have ridden from London,” Harcourt said, “because in six weeks the Crown is going to send a committee of very serious gentlemen into this very serious house, and if they do not like what they find, you will spend the rest of your life as the duke who turned away the soldiers.”
The room went quiet in the way that rooms did when a thing had been said that could not be unsaid.
Alexander reached for the teapot, not because he wanted tea but because his hands required an occupation that was not making fists, and he poured a cup he had no intention of drinking.
“Explain yourself,” he said. “Plainly, if you are capable of it.”
So Harcourt explained.

There was a charity, he said, got up under royal patronage and no small amount of noble money, to make a home for the soldiers and sailors broken in the late wars, the ones the great hospitals at Greenwich and Chelsea could not hold. They wanted houses. Great houses, in healthful country, with grounds a convalescent man might walk in and rooms enough to fill with beds.

“And someone, in their wisdom, has put your name forward,” Harcourt went on. “Wrenwick Hall, a great house standing all but empty, with a master too well known to be quietly passed over and too little seen to be quietly approved. A committee has been formed to choose among the houses offered. Yours is on the list whether you offered it or not.”
“I did not offer it,” Alexander said sharply.
“I am aware. Someone offered it for you.” Alexander let the silence work, watching his friend. “You have the look of a man who already knows whose hand it was.”

“I have the look of a man who has not breakfasted, which you persist in confusing with guilt.” But Harcourt did not quite meet his eye, and set the orange down with more care than the fruit required. “They come in six weeks to see whether the house is fit. And whether the duke is.”
“And if I decline the honour?”

“Then you decline, very publicly, to give comfortable rooms to men who lost their legs at Waterloo so that you might keep yours sealed and empty. You decline in front of a committee that answers to people who answer to the Regent.”
He met Alexander’s eyes directly, and the wit had gone out of him, which was always how Alexander knew his friend was in earnest.

“You have spent five years letting the world believe whatever it likes about you. Mad, they say. Cursed. Cruel. I have heard all three at the same dinner, from the same woman, between the soup and the fish. You have never once troubled to correct any of it, and I have never understood why, but I have held my tongue because it was your grief and not my business. This is different. Refuse this, and the story stops being whispered. It gets written down. It gets entered in the minutes of a Crown committee, and from there it is only a short walk to the papers, and a duke can survive being whispered about for a lifetime and not survive being printed about for a fortnight.”
Alexander said nothing.
The cup of tea cooled in front of him, the steam thinning to nothing, and beyond the window the sky made up its mind and let down a fine grey rain upon the limes.
The trouble was not the committee. He had faced worse rooms than a committee.

The trouble was that a house fit to receive convalescent soldiers was a house with no doors locked against the world, and there was a door in the west wing that he had not opened in five years, and behind it the smell of smoke still lived in the plaster. He did not know, sitting here in the cold civil morning, whether he was the kind of man who could open it or the kind who would let men suffer rather than try.
“You have gone somewhere I cannot follow,” Harcourt observed, more quietly. “You do that now. You did not used to.”
“I am thinking,” he said, after too long a pause.

“You are leaving the room without standing up. It is a newer trick and I do not care for it.” Harcourt let the moment sit, then chose, with the tact that he hid so well beneath the noise that most people never suspected he owned any, to change his ground. “What is it you imagine you require, to be ready in six weeks?”
“An army of competent strangers and rather less conscience.”

“You require a housekeeper,” Harcourt said. “A real one. Not another terrified girl who lasts a fortnight and leaves in the night without her wages because she would rather forfeit them than ask you for them. You need a woman who can take a house in this condition and have it standing to attention by midsummer, and who will not faint at the sight of you, and who will not be impressed by the silver.”
“I have had housekeepers.”
“You have had victims. There is a difference, and it is chiefly that the victims left.”

Alexander rose and went to the window, where he might rest his eyes on the rain instead of his friend’s face. The weather had settled into a steady grey that suited his temper better than the room did.

“Very well. Find me one. Someone of sense. Young enough to climb the stairs of this house without making a martyrdom of it, and old enough not to be dazzled by the address. A widow, perhaps. Widows tend to have made their peace with disappointment, and I have a good deal of it to offer.”
There was a pause behind him, and then Harcourt’s voice, far too pleased with itself.
“Do you know, Wrenwick, I came in here expecting to persuade you to engage a domestic servant. I had not understood I was to assist you in designing your ideal woman.”
“I asked for a housekeeper, not a humorist.”

“You asked for a sensible widow, unimpressed by rank, capable in a crisis, immune to your considerable charm, and indifferent to wealth. Shall I enquire whether she ought also to be handsome, or will you affect not to mind?”

“I asked,” said Alexander, with the particular evenness he used when he wished a subject closed, “for thirty-two functioning servants and have instead been given the conversational range of a matchmaking aunt. Find me someone competent, Harcourt. I do not greatly care what she looks like, provided she can make this house stop flinching before the Crown arrives to watch it do so.”

He did not turn from the window as he said it. If he had examined the list of qualities he had just recited, he suspected it would not have borne examining, and so he chose not to examine it, and watched the rain instead.

“You might at least pretend to be grateful,” Harcourt said, gathering his gloves. “I am about to perform a small miracle on your behalf, and I shall expect to be fed for it, and housed, and very probably thanked, though I have learned to take the thanks on a long credit.”
“You will be housed. The thanks I shall keep in reserve until I see whether your miracle can run a still-room.”

“She can run a still-room, an army, and a man of your peculiar difficulty, or I am no judge, and I am an excellent judge of everything but my own affairs.” Harcourt paused at the door, and the smile in his voice was the kind Alexander had learned, over twenty years, to mistrust on principle. “As it happens, I know exactly the woman.”
And then, more quietly, almost to himself, like a man laying down a small private wager he fully expected to win, he added, “God help the pair of you.”

the-rakish-viscounts-pretend-wife.heading: Chapter One: The Oaf in Her Bed
paras: “Sir, you are in my bed.”

The man did not so much as twitch. He lay sprawled on his back across the narrow mattress, one boot on, one boot off, snoring with a deep, wet, rattling enthusiasm that suggested his body was attempting to expel his soul through his nostrils.
Delilah Pearce stood three feet away, dripping melted snow onto the floorboards of the room she had paid for, and addressed him in a tone that could have stripped paint from a warship.
“Sir. You are in my room, in my bed, and I will thank you to remove yourself from both.”
The snoring hitched, stuttered, and resumed at a louder volume, which she had not thought possible.

She set her traveling case down with a deliberate thud. Six years of careful, relentless, soul-crushing propriety, and it was all going to come undone because some man had decided to collapse across her bed at a coaching inn in the middle of a snowstorm. He occupied roughly three-fifths of the mattress, his cravat hanging loose around his neck like a surrendered flag, his coat tossed over the chair with the accuracy of a man who had aimed for the floor and missed upward.

She crossed to the bed and looked at his face properly for the first time, and a small lurch of irritation went through her at the discovery that he was not hideous. Of course he wasn’t. The situation was apparently insufficiently absurd without the added indignity of the intruder being handsome. Dark hair fell across his forehead, the lashes were absurd, the nose a strong Roman line, the features so well proportioned it was frankly sickening.
“Sir, wake up at once.” She prodded his shoulder.

He made a sound that was half groan, half word, and rolled onto his side, presenting her with a broad expanse of back. His shirt had come untucked. A strip of bare skin showed above his waistband, and Delilah looked at the ceiling so quickly she nearly strained her neck.
One more attempt, this time with the sharp end of her elbow against his arm.
“Mmrph,” he contributed.
Very well. The innkeeper, then.

The corridor was freezing, the stairs groaned under her feet, and the taproom at the bottom was crowded with stranded travelers steaming gently by the fire. Mr. Briggs, the innkeeper, was wiping down the bar with the focused intensity of a man who had been wiping that same bar for thirty years and intended to die doing it.
“Mr. Briggs.” She used the precise, measured tone she had perfected over six years of managing other people’s terrible children. “There is a man in my room.”
Mr. Briggs looked up and blinked at her. “Aye, that’ll be your husband, ma’am.”
The floor tilted.
Her feet stayed planted and her spine stayed straight, but inside her skull her thoughts performed a rapid and undignified scramble, like an alley cat dropped into a bathtub.
“I beg your pardon? My what?”

“The gentleman who came in earlier. Paid for the room, said he was expecting his wife on the later coach.” Mr. Briggs shrugged. “That’d be you, then, ma’am. Last coach through before the road closed. There’ll be no more tonight, nor tomorrow neither, by the look of that sky.”
It would not, in fact, be her, and Delilah opened her mouth to say exactly that.
Then she stopped.

Behind Mr. Briggs, the taproom was half full of strangers, and a stout woman by the fire had already glanced over twice with the bright, hungry interest of a person collecting material. If Delilah said what she was about to say, the calculation ran as follows. A single woman, a strange man, one room, one bed, and no possible way to leave. The truth would need explaining, and explaining was already ruin. By the time the story traveled the thirty miles to the Hargrove estate it would have grown teeth. Miss Pearce, who spent the night with a man at a coaching inn. Miss Pearce, dismissed before she had hung up her cloak.

And there was no fourth position waiting behind this one. The letter from Mrs. Bell’s registry office sat folded at the bottom of her trunk, and she could recite it without looking. Given the circumstances of your last departure, we consider ourselves generous in putting you forward at all. We trust there will be no further difficulties. The circumstances had been a seventeen-year-old boy’s wandering hands and his mother’s conviction that the governess must have invited them, and the whisper of it had followed Delilah through eight months of rejections before the Hargroves condescended to engage her. Mrs. Hargrove’s letter of engagement had used the word spotless twice in one paragraph.

Two pounds, eleven shillings, and fourpence. That was what stood between Delilah Pearce and the workhouse, and all of it was sewn into the hem of a gray dress upstairs in a room that currently contained a snoring stranger.

So Delilah, who had not told a deliberate lie in six years, who had built her entire survival on being correct and proper and beyond reproach, looked Mr. Briggs in the eye and said, “Of course. Yes. My husband. I confess I did not expect him to have arrived before me.”
The words tasted like ash and burnt toast.
“Only,” she continued, “the room is rather small, and my husband, you understand, snores like a dying bullock. Might there be a second room available? Purely for the sake of my rest.”
Mr. Briggs laughed. He actually laughed, as though she had made a joke. “Bless you, ma’am, we’ve been full since midday. Storm’s driven half the county indoors. You’re lucky to have a room at all.”
“Lucky,” Delilah repeated. “Yes. I feel it very keenly. How long do such storms generally last, Mr. Briggs?”

“This one?” He gave the question the consideration of a professional. “Three days, by the smell of it. Maybe four. The mail won’t try the hill again till the drifts come down, and the Bath road’s shut both ways. You picked a fine night for traveling, ma’am, and that’s a fact.”
“I did not pick it. It picked me.”
“Aye, well. Weather’s like marriage that way, ma’am, if you’ll pardon my saying so. A body doesn’t choose it so much as get caught out in it.”
“That is remarkably philosophical, Mr. Briggs.”
“It’s the storm, ma’am. Brings it out of a man.”
“Mrs. Briggs will send up a bit of supper. Can’t have a new bride going hungry.” He winked at her. He winked. “We can always tell the new ones, ma’am. You’ve that look about you.”
“Have I? How observant you are, Mr. Briggs.”
She climbed the stairs with her chin up and her heart in full rebellion behind her stays, back to a room that now contained her luggage, her exhaustion, and a husband she had never met.

He had shifted in her absence. Flat on his back again, one arm flung above his head, shirt riding higher than before, and she gave the washstand her full attention. The washstand was a respectable object that inspired no feelings whatsoever.

She was weighing her options, which ranged from sleeping in the chair to smothering him with his own coat, when he stirred. His chest rose on a deep breath and he made a low, rough sound in his throat, the sound of a man surfacing from a very deep sleep, and the gravelly warmth of it landed in her chest like a dropped stone.
Oh, her brain supplied, unbidden and unhelpful. So that is what a man sounds like when he wakes.
She buried the observation under the sharpest tone she could muster.
“Good evening. I trust you have enjoyed your rest in my bed.”
His eyes opened. Gray, or possibly green. The candlelight made it difficult to say, and she had no intention of getting close enough to settle the question.

He blinked at her. Blinked at the ceiling. Then he turned his head and looked at her again, slowly, and a smile started at one corner of his mouth with the lazy confidence of a man who smiled often and to great effect.
“Well,” he said, his voice sleep-rough and warm. She hated every syllable of it. “This is a pleasant surprise.”
“I assure you, sir, it is no such thing.”

“You’re certain? From where I’m lying it has every appearance of one.” He pushed himself up against the headboard and dragged a hand through his hair, which made it worse and better at the same time. “Forgive me. Do I know you? I feel I’d remember.”
“We have never met, and you are in my room.”

“Am I?” He looked around with the careful, squinting assessment of a man piecing together a puzzle through a headache. “That’s odd. The innkeeper assigned me this room. I have a distinct memory of stairs.”
“The innkeeper assigned me this room. I have a receipt.”
“I may also have a receipt. Somewhere.” He patted his coat pockets, discovered he was not wearing his coat, and abandoned the search. “Though I confess I’m not entirely certain I remember paying.”
“You were drunk.”
“I was relaxed.”
“You were unconscious, sir. I prodded you with my elbow and you said, and I quote, mmrph.”
“That doesn’t sound like me. I’m told I’m very eloquent.”
“By whom, precisely?”
“Myself, chiefly. The testimony of others has been mixed.”
“I begin to see why.”

“Most people require a fortnight to see why. You are quick, wife.” He frowned at his single boot, then at his bare foot, as if the two facts could not be made to agree. “Where, precisely, has the evening gone? Last I recall it was afternoon and I was having a perfectly civilized disagreement with a bottle of brandy.”
“The brandy appears to have won.”

“It usually does. That’s what makes it civilized.” He looked up at her then, and something sharpened behind the sleepiness, some quality of attention she would have preferred he not possess. “You’re soaked through and white as the tablecloth, and you’re standing in a room with a strange man instead of demanding the innkeeper throw me into the snow. Something is wrong.”
It would have been easier if he were stupid. She had been counting on stupid.
“There has been a complication,” she said.
“I’m very good at complications. They’re my chief occupation.”
“The innkeeper believes you are my husband.”
A pause. His eyebrows climbed. “Does he, indeed.”

“You apparently informed him, while relaxed, that you expected your wife on the later coach. I was the only woman on the later coach. The inn is full, the road is closed, and the storm is expected to last days.” She folded her hands at her waist, the picture of composure, while her pulse hammered against her collar. “There is no other room to be had, and a single woman discovered sharing this one with a stranger is ruined the moment the discovery is made. So I did not correct him.”

He absorbed this in silence, and she braced for the responses experience had taught her to expect from gentlemen. The leer. The bargain. The smug, slow assessment of what her predicament might be worth to him.
Instead he said, “What’s my name?”
“I beg your pardon?”

“My name. If I’m to be your husband, you’ll want to know what to call me, and I’d rather not learn from the innkeeper that I’ve been rechristened Archibald.” He swung his legs over the side of the bed and sat there, rumpled and one-booted, regarding her with an expression of grave helpfulness somewhat undermined by the state of his hair. “Simon Cathcart. At your service, madam, evidently in a more permanent capacity than either of us anticipated.”
“Delilah Pearce.”

He turned her name over once, silently, as though testing the weight of it, and she chose not to notice what his face did while he was about it. “And how long have we been married, Mrs. Cathcart? These details matter. The innkeeper’s wife will ask. Innkeepers’ wives always ask.”
“As briefly as possible.”
“A month, then. Married one month, traveling to visit your relations, and I am devoted to you.”
“Mildly attached will suffice.”
“I am incapable of mild attachment. It is a defect of the bloodline.”
“Then feign moderation. You claim to be charming, and charm is nine parts moderation.”
“Whoever told you that has never charmed anyone in their life.”
“A whirlwind courtship, then. I like us already.”
A knock landed on the door, brisk and proprietary, and before either of them had moved it swung open to reveal a sturdy woman with a tray, flour on her sleeve and frank curiosity everywhere else.
“Supper,” she announced. “Bread, stew, and the last of the apple tart, on account of you being newlyweds. I’m Mrs. Briggs. It cheers a storm up wonderfully, having a young couple in the house.”
“You are very kind,” Delilah said.

Mrs. Briggs set the tray down and surveyed them both with the satisfaction of a woman confirming a theory. “Briggs said to me, that’s a couple not long married, and I said I should think not, look at them, still shy of each other across a room.” She beamed. “How did you meet, then?”
“At a dinner party,” Delilah said.
“In a snowstorm,” Simon said, at the same moment.
The silence lasted half a heartbeat. Mrs. Briggs blinked.
“A dinner party,” Delilah said, with tremendous composure, “during a snowstorm. The weather is rather a theme with us.”
“Well, isn’t that romantic,” said Mrs. Briggs, satisfied, and saw herself out, and the door had barely latched before Delilah rounded on him.
“In what conceivable world was that a helpful answer?”
“It was the first true thing that came to mind. I panicked. You were magnificent.”
“We will rehearse,” she said grimly. “You will learn our entire history before you sleep, and you will keep to it, or you will sink us both inside a day.”
“I look forward to discovering how we fell in love. Spare no detail.”

He bent to retrieve his other boot from the floor, swayed, thought better of bending, and straightened with dignity. “Well, wife. You may as well give me the rules. A woman who can construct an entire marriage in the space of a staircase has rules, and I’d rather hear them now than discover them one at a time.”

Delilah looked at him, at the loose cravat and the wicked, patient amusement, and a thought arrived with the cold clarity of the snow against the window. Her position, her registry, her two pounds and eleven shillings, the whole narrow architecture of her survival, now rested on the discretion of a man who could not remember paying for the room he was found unconscious in.

“Rule the first,” she said. “You will sleep on the left side of the bed, against the wall, and you will stay there as though your life depends upon it. Because, Mr. Cathcart, I promise you that it does.”
“And rule the second?”
“You will discover the rules as you break them. It appears to be the only pace at which you learn.”
“Married four hours,” he said, to the ceiling, “and already she knows me better than my own mother.”
His smile spread, slow and delighted, and she understood with sinking certainty that she had just made everything immeasurably worse.
“Mrs. Cathcart,” he said, “I believe this is going to be the most interesting marriage of my life.”

twelve-days-to-keep-an-earl.heading: Chapter One: The Yew Tree Bargain
paras: *Christmas Eve, 1815*

Mr. Ambrose Fallow had been seated beside Goldie Peverell on the drawing room sofa with all the subtlety of a cannon wheeled onto a croquet lawn, and for the better part of an hour he had been discharging compliments at her in a slow and solemn barrage.

“You enjoy a robust constitution, Miss Peverell,” he observed, studying her over the rim of his teacup as a farmer might study a promising heifer. “I remarked upon it to your mother at dinner. A lady of sturdy health is a great comfort in a household. Both my late wives were delicate.”
“Were they, sir?” Goldie balanced a mince pie on her saucer and wondered how much of it could be eaten before he drew breath again. “How inconvenient for you.”

“It was a trial, and I bore it with patience.” He inclined his head, accepting a sympathy she had never offered. “Health, however, is merely the foundation. Upon it a good husband may build. A little gentle correction of the enthusiasms, a moderating of the voice, and I daresay the result would be most creditable.”

The Peverell drawing room was hot enough to ripen fruit. Every neighbor within walking distance had come in out of the snow for the squire’s Christmas Eve punch, the fire had been built for a siege, and her young brothers Ned and Kit were crawling beneath the pianoforte in pursuit of a spaniel that had stolen a glove. By the hearth her father was telling the vicar his story about the goose and the bishop, a story Goldie had heard every Christmas of her life and had yet to sit through with a straight face.
She laughed at the bishop’s wig precisely where she always did, and the sound rolled across the room and rattled the spoons.
Her mother’s eyebrows rose from behind the tea urn like two small flags of warning.
Mr. Fallow set down his cup. “There, you see. An excellent example of the enthusiasm I mentioned.”
“My laugh, sir?”
“Its volume,” he said gravely. “In York a lady’s amusement is generally expressed by a smile, and on occasions of great hilarity, by a second smile.”
“Then York must be a restful place to tell a joke.”

“It is a place of order, Miss Peverell, and I flatter myself that my own house is the most orderly in it.” He drew a breath that swelled his waistcoat alarmingly. “Indeed, since we have the evening before us and the roads are closed, I propose that you and I pass it in discussing the orderly management of a future household. I have prepared several heads of argument. The first concerns the keys.”
Goldie had sworn to her mother that very morning that she would be civil to Mr. Fallow until Twelfth Night, and she had meant every word. She rose from the sofa before he reached the keys.
“How thoughtful of you, sir, and how very unlucky that I have just remembered the church candles.”
“At this hour?”

“For the midnight service. I promised Mr. Dunn they would be counted.” The vicar, ten feet away and deep in the goose, was in no position to contradict her. “It cannot wait, and I would never forgive myself if you took a chill by coming with me.”

She was through the door before her mother’s eyebrows could travel any higher. Her emerald velvet pelisse hung on its peg in the hall, and she dragged it on over her evening gown without stopping for a bonnet, then let herself out into the snow.

The cold was glorious. It had been falling since the day before, thick and steady, and the green lay buried to the tops of the mounting blocks while every cottage window along the High Street burned gold. Goldie picked up her skirts and waded across to the lych-gate, her slippers soaking through at once, her breath streaming behind her. She had no intention of counting a single candle. The old yew at the corner of the churchyard had sheltered her from governesses, aunts and one very determined gander, and its branches hung low enough tonight to hide a coach and four.
She ducked beneath them at a run and collided with a wall that grunted.
Two hands caught her elbows and kept her upright. The wall wore a greatcoat, smelled of cold air and oranges, and stood a good deal taller than any man in Hollybourne had a right to.
“Steady,” it said. “I am afraid this tree is taken. There is a very roomy headstone to your left.”
Eight years had dropped that voice by half an octave and done nothing else to it. Goldie stood perfectly still while snow slid off the branch above and down the back of her collar.
“Jules Everleigh, you wretch,” she said.
“Good evening, Marigold.”
“Do not call me that.”

“It is your name. I was there when the vicar wrote it in the register, or near enough.” He let go of her elbows, rather slowly, and tipped his head to see her by the gleam off the snow. He had been a lanky, laughing boy of eighteen when he left. The man under the yew had shoulders that blocked out a gravestone and the same disgraceful grin, and his hair, even in the dark, was the color of a new guinea. “You have grown.”
“So have you. I see nobody thought to stop you.”
“They tried, in London. I proved resistant.” He was smiling down at her as though she were a favorite view. “The last time I stood this near you, I believe you were pushing me into the millpond.”
“You had called my hair a fire hazard.”
“I meant it as a compliment. I was eighteen and very bad at them.”
“You have had eight years to improve.”
“I have used them diligently.” He put his head on one side. “Your hair is still a fire hazard, Marigold, and Yorkshire has been a great deal too dark without it.”

Her cheeks warmed in spite of the snow, and she was grateful for the shadow of the branches. Three Seasons in London had taught her exactly what a gentleman’s compliment was worth, and it was unreasonable that this one should still land.
“That is no better than the first attempt,” she told him briskly.
“Give me until Twelfth Night.” He glanced past her toward the lit windows of the green. “May I ask what you are running from? You came in like a cavalry charge.”
“A magistrate.”
“Good Lord. What have you done?”

“It is what he wishes to do. He wishes to marry me and then correct me.” She shook the snow out of her collar. “His name is Mr. Fallow, and he believes a wife ought to be quiet, grateful and decorative. I have disappointed him on all three counts before the soup.”
Jules laughed. It was a real laugh, sudden and too loud for a churchyard, and he smothered it against his glove. “Is he always so solemn, or has he saved his finest misery for Christmas?”
“He has a great store of it. He rations nothing.” Goldie folded her arms over the pelisse. “And you, my lord? Earls do not commonly lurk under trees on Christmas Eve. When did you come?”
“An hour ago.”
“And you have not shown yourself at a single door.”

“I have shown myself at one. My steward met me on the step with a ledger under each arm and a face like a wet haystack.” His shoulder moved under the greatcoat. “I told him I wished to pay my respects at my father’s grave and walked out again. Tibbs is a patient man, but I doubt he will wait in the hall much longer.”
“So that was an excuse.”
“It is over there.” He did not turn his head toward it. “I have been meaning to walk across for some time. The tree had better conversation.”

Goldie had a sharp remark ready on the subject of sons who stayed away eight years and came home after dark, and she kept it behind her teeth. There had been shouting at the Hall the night he left. Half the village had heard it, and the other half had been told by morning.
“They have not forgiven your father, you know,” she said instead. “The roofs, the mill, the wages. You will find the village civil and very cold.”
“I do not need them warm. I need them to leave me in peace for a fortnight.” He said it lightly, and then spoiled the effect at once. “Is old Gable still alive? And Pike’s father, at the forge?”
“For a man who wants no dealings with the village, you ask a great many questions about it.”
“Idle curiosity.”
“Mr. Gable is alive and angrier than ever. Old Mr. Pike died three winters ago, and Gideon has the smithy now.” She watched him take that in, his jaw working once. “You might have written, Jules.”
“I might have done a great many things.”
A lantern swung into view beyond the lych-gate, and a voice of terrible patience carried across the graves.
“Miss Peverell? Miss Peverell, your mother is anxious. I have brought a shawl, and a few observations on the imprudence of night air.”
Goldie seized Jules by the sleeve and dragged him deeper under the branches. “That is him. Do not breathe.”
“He has a lantern. He will follow your footprints straight to us.”
“Then I shall climb the tree.”

“In slippers?” Jules considered the swaying light for a moment, and a look came over his face that she remembered from the summer he had talked her into borrowing the miller’s boat. “Let us give him a new subject to think about.”
“Jules Everleigh, if you are about to say what I think you are about to say, I will push you into the nearest open grave.”
“You may push me afterward.”
He took her hand, tucked it firmly through his arm, and walked her out from under the yew into the full light of Mr. Fallow’s lantern.
“Good evening, sir,” he called, as warmly as if they had met in a ballroom. “You must be the gentleman from York. I am Wintermere. Miss Peverell has been telling me all about you.”

Mr. Fallow stopped so suddenly that the shawl slid off his arm into the snow. His eyes traveled from the stranger’s hat to the stranger’s boots and then to Goldie’s hand, lying on a sleeve of superfine where it had no business to be.
“You are the earl?” he said. “I understood his lordship to be fixed in London.”

“He was, and he has thought better of it. You see before you Miss Peverell’s most devoted admirer these many years.” Jules beamed at him. “You will forgive my stealing her away from the party. I had been from home so long that I could not wait until morning to pay my addresses, which are of the most earnest kind.”
“This is exceedingly irregular,” said Mr. Fallow faintly.
“It is Christmas Eve, sir. I hoped the season would excuse me.”

Goldie’s face had gone hot to the roots of her hair, and she fixed her eyes on the church tower for fear of what they would do to either gentleman. Mr. Fallow bowed, retrieved the shawl, bowed a second time with snow dripping from the fringe, and remarked that Mrs. Peverell would wish to be informed. He retreated toward the green at a pace just short of a trot.
Goldie waited until the lantern had passed the lych-gate. Then she pulled her hand free and struck the Earl of Wintermere in the chest with the flat of it.
“Are you out of your senses?”
“You are welcome.”

“He will tell my mother. He is telling her now. By the time I reach the house she will have chosen the hymns.” She struck him again, since the first blow had made so little impression. “I asked you for nothing, Jules. I have handled that man alone since the day he arrived, and I would have handled him until the day he left.”
“By hiding under a tree.”
“It is a very good tree!”

“It is,” he agreed. “I have every respect for it.” He rubbed his chest where she had hit him, and for once the grin slipped sideways into an expression far less certain. “Listen to me a moment before you fetch the shovel. I had better tell you why I am home.”
“I assumed you had run out of tailors.”
“I am selling Wintermere.”
The churchyard was very still. Up in the tower the ringers had begun to gather for the midnight peal, and a single bell gave a soft, uncertain note as a rope was tried.
“You are not,” Goldie said.
“After Twelfth Night. There is a buyer, and the papers are drawn.”

“That house has been Everleigh land since before the church had a roof. There are farms on it that have gone from father to son longer than anybody can remember. There is Mrs. Gable’s cottage and the Fenners’ grazing and the mill.” Her voice was climbing, and she let it climb. “You cannot hand all that to a stranger, like a horse that has gone lame.”

“I can, and I must, and I would be obliged if you did not ask me why tonight.” He spoke pleasantly, with his gaze on the snow between them. “What I need is for it to go smoothly. A village that already hates the name can make a sale very ugly, with petitions and broken windows and tenants who will not treat with the new man. I would like to leave them better disposed than I found them, and nobody in this dale understands how to manage that better than you.”
“I do not manage people.”
“Goldie, you had the churchwardens in hand at eleven.”
“I advised them.”

“And they found themselves buying a new bell rope.” He drew a breath and let it go in a cloud. “So here is my offer. A courtship, until Twelfth Night. I pay you every attention in public, and your magistrate goes home to York with his heads of argument unspoken. In return you walk me through the village and tell me whose hand to shake. You keep your freedom, and I keep my neck.”
“And what do I get out of it, besides your company, which I have survived without for eight years?”
“My undying gratitude.”
“I would rather have your hat. My ears are freezing.”
He took off his hat at once and set it on her head. It came down over her eyebrows and smelled of oranges, and she pushed it back with one finger so that she could go on glaring at him.

It was a shameless proposal from a shameless man, and every sensible instinct she possessed ought to have rejected it. She was counting on her fingers inside the pelisse instead. Twelve days lay between tonight and Twelfth Night, and there were carols tomorrow, baskets on Boxing Day, the millpond frozen hard enough to skate upon. A man could be shown a great deal of Hollybourne in twelve days if the right person did the showing.

“Until Twelfth Night, then,” she said. “You will come to church in the morning, in your own pew, and sing. You will call on whoever I tell you to call on. And you will make no promise to a single tenant that you do not mean to keep.”
“You drive a hard bargain for a woman in my hat.”
“Those are my terms.”
“Then I accept them.” He held out his hand, and she shook it as she would have shaken a farmer’s at market. His glove closed around hers and stayed a moment longer than a bargain required.

“One thing more,” Goldie said, taking her hand back. “This is a pretense, and it ends when the cake is cut. I will never marry a man who needs managing, Jules. I have told my mother so every spring for three years. You need not fear I shall grow fond of the arrangement.”
“I should not dream of fearing it,” he said meekly.

They walked back through the lych-gate with a careful yard of snow between them. On the green the squire’s windows blazed, and the shadow of her mother could be seen crossing and recrossing the drawing room curtains at speed.
“She will want to hear your intentions,” Goldie warned him.
“I shall tell her they are honorable and seasonal.”
“You will tell her nothing clever at all. You will bow, and admire the punch, and let me do the talking.”
“For a lady who does not manage people, you have a remarkable command of the imperative.”

“Hold your tongue.” At the foot of the steps she turned to inspect him, as she would have inspected Ned before church. His cravat had been tied in London by a valet and then dragged through a yew tree, and it sat a full inch off the true. Her hands went up before she had given them leave. She tugged the knot straight, smoothed the linen flat beneath his chin, and tucked the ends inside his waistcoat with two brisk pats.

Jules had stopped breathing. He stood on her father’s bottom step as still as the church tower, his chin lifted and his eyes on a point above her borrowed hat, and when she took her hands away they were less steady than they had been.
“There,” she said. “You were crooked.”
“So I have often been told.”
Neither of them mentioned it again, and Goldie opened the door on the heat and the noise and her mother’s astonished face.

twelve-nights-to-trust-a-duke.heading: Prologue: The Weight of Ink
paras: *Five years earlier*
The study at Marlby parsonage had not been warm since Michaelmas, and Harriet Lisle had put on her pelisse to hear her father explain why they must leave it.

He sat behind the desk where he had written a thousand sermons. The lawyer’s letter lay open on the blotter between them, a single sheet in a clerk’s clean hand, and beside it lay the builder’s account for the new church roof, which ran to four sheets and had been delivered that morning by the builder himself.

“I do not understand it, Papa,” she said. “I have read the letter thrice. They write that the present duke’s men of business have searched the late duke’s papers and can discover no record of any endowment to this parish. But he stood in our own churchyard and promised it. I was there. He pointed at the roof with his cane.”
“He did, my dear.”
“He said the living should be made secure, and the school built, and that you were to begin the repairs at once and send the reckoning to him. You had his Grace’s word.”

“Given before witnesses,” said Mr. Lisle. He took off his spectacles and polished them on his cuff, which he did when he could not meet a person’s eye. “The churchwardens heard it. So did the curate, and half the vestry. He gave it on his honor as a gentleman.”
“Then why did you not have his signature?”
“Because I believed him.”

He said it very simply. He was the best man she had ever known, and he had borrowed in his own name to mend a roof that was not his, on the strength of a few sentences spoken across a wet churchyard by a great nobleman with a cane. The nobleman had died of an apoplexy before the slates were on. Now the builder wanted paying, and the bishop had written with regret, and the son and heir in London had never heard of Marlby in his life.
Harriet was one-and-twenty. She had kept the parish registers since she was fourteen, in a hand neater than the curate’s, and she had never yet entered a baptism without the date.
“Belief will not keep the roof on, Papa.”
“No.”

“There was a pen in the vestry. There was ink. It would have taken his Grace less time than it took him to climb back into his carriage.” Her voice was level, and she kept it so with some effort. “I am not reproaching you. I only wish to learn how it was done. A man of sense and learning, undone by a thing a child might have prevented. I want to see where the mistake lies, so that I shall recognize it.”
“You think it a mistake to take a man at his word...”

“I think a word weighs nothing. It is air. One may say anything, and afterward one may die, or forget, or find it inconvenient.” She laid one finger on the builder’s account. “Ink has weight. This has weight. Mr. Tarrant wrote down every slate.”
Her father regarded her for a long moment over the bare desk. He appeared older than he had at breakfast, and there was a grayness about his mouth that she did not like.
“It is a cold creed for a girl of your age, Harriet,” he said gently.
“It is a cold study.”

She went round the desk and kissed his forehead, since she had not meant to wound him and could see that she had. Then she sat down in the curate’s chair, drew the builder’s account toward her, and began to copy it out fair. They would need a copy. In her experience people who owed a debt were always asked, sooner or later, to prove what they had already paid.
The lesson went in deep that afternoon.
*Christmas Eve, 1815*
The postilion had declared at the last tollgate that only a scholar or a lunatic would attempt the dale road in such weather, and Harriet, who had been called both, had told him to drive on.

She regretted it somewhat by the fourth mile. The hired chaise labored upward between walls of snow, the horses plunging to their knees, the lamps showing nothing ahead but a white whirl. Far below and behind them the lights of a village called Hollybourne had dwindled to a handful of sparks and gone out. She sat with her feet on her trunk to keep them from the wet straw and held her father’s Greek lexicon in her lap, as another woman might have held a lapdog.

She was six-and-twenty. She owned the trunk, the lexicon, three notebooks, a magnifying glass on a ribbon, and one good gown of gold silk that had been her mother’s. She also possessed a letter of engagement from the Duke of Ravensmoor’s secretary, signed, dated and witnessed, which she had read through twice more at the last change of horses.

She had not wished to work for a Ravensmoor. She had turned the letter over for a week before she answered it. But a scholar without fortune went where the books were, and the North Library at Thornleigh was spoken of in the same breath as Althorp, and the fee would keep her father in his lodgings at Harrogate through another winter of the waters.
The house came out of the storm all at once, a great dark cliff of stone with a single row of windows alight. A door opened. A lantern was raised.
“Miss Lisle! You have achieved the impossible. We had given you up to the drifts.”

The gentleman who handed her down was fair, slender and perhaps five-and-thirty, with a pleasant, mobile face and a coat a good deal finer than a secretary’s salary generally allowed. He bowed over her wet glove as though it had been a duchess’s.

“Alistair Finch, ma’am, his Grace’s secretary, and entirely at your service. You must be perished. There is a fire in the small parlor and a hot supper to follow, and I have had the Blue Room aired, since it is nearest the library and I am told that scholars do not care to be parted from their subject.”
“You are very good, sir. Is the duke in residence?”

“His Grace is detained in London,” Mr. Finch said, with a small apologetic smile. “He is seldom anywhere else. I do not believe he has set foot in Thornleigh since he was a boy. He leaves the library entirely to your judgment.”
“Then I trust he has also left you the keys.”
“Naturally.”
“Excellent. I should hate to catalogue a locked door.”

Mr. Finch laughed, a little late. Behind him a tall woman in black bombazine had come out onto the step with a shawl over her cap, and she took in the visitor, the trunk and the lexicon in one sweep of a pair of shrewd gray eyes.
“Mrs. Mabbott, the housekeeper,” said the secretary. “She will see to your comfort.”

“I will see to her feet first. They are wet through.” Mrs. Mabbott lifted the trunk out of the chaise with one hand, as if it had been a workbasket. “Only a scholar or a lunatic travels north at Christmas, miss. Which are you?”
“The postilion asked me the same question,” Harriet said. “I told him I would send word when I had finished the catalogue.”
The housekeeper’s mouth twitched at one corner.
“You’ll do,” she said, and led the way in out of the snow.

more.heading: Night One: The Brute and the Bluestocking
paras: *Christmas Eve*
Mrs. Mabbott had been firm on the subject of wet wool.
“That traveling dress goes to the laundry maid, miss, and it does not come back until it is dry through. Have you nothing else?”
“A gray stuff gown, in the trunk. I am afraid the snow came in at the lid.”
“Then that goes down too. And this?”

The housekeeper had lifted the tissue from the bottom of the trunk. The gold silk lay beneath it, folded as Harriet’s mother had folded it twenty years ago, heavy and old-fashioned and still the color of a candle flame.
“It is an evening gown,” Harriet said. “I brought it because I could not think where to leave it. I had not meant to wear it to catalogue books.”
“It is the only dry thing you own. You may wear it or sit by the parlor fire in a blanket until morning.”
“I came here to work, Mrs. Mabbott. I do not waste evenings.”
“Then you had better let me do up the hooks,” said the housekeeper.

So it was in gold silk, with her hair pinned flat and her magnifying glass on its ribbon round her neck, that Harriet Lisle first walked into the North Library of Thornleigh. She stopped a yard inside the door with her candle held up and forgot, for the space of a full minute, to be cold.

It was a room built by somebody who had loved books better than people. It ran the entire width of the house, forty paces from end to end, and it rose through two stories to a coved ceiling lost in shadow. A gallery ran round it halfway up, reached by a spiral stair in each corner. Every wall was books. They stood in ranks from the floor to the cornice, calf and vellum and red morocco, and the light of her one candle woke a thousand small gleams of gilt and went out among them like a pebble dropped down a well.
“Oh,” Harriet said, to nobody. “Oh, you beauties.”

She walked the length of it slowly. The fire at the far end had been lit for her, and four great lamps burned on the reading tables, and by their glow she began, from habit, to take the measure of the place. There was dust on the upper shelves and none on the lower. The carpet was worn in a path between the door and the locked glass cases on the north wall. In the bay marked for the Greek and Latin classics, a row of folios leaned a little, as books lean when their neighbors have lately been pulled out and pushed back by a careless hand.
She did not waste evenings. She set down her candle, opened the first of her notebooks, and wrote the date at the head of the page.
The Sophocles came to hand within the hour.

It stood in the classics bay at the height of her shoulder, a small thick octavo in dark red morocco, with the anchor and dolphin of the Aldine press stamped in gold upon the cover. She drew it out with both hands. It was the first printed edition of the seven tragedies, made in Venice more than three hundred years ago, and she had seen one other copy in her life, through glass, in the Bodleian.

The spine was right. She turned it to the lamp and it was beautifully, convincingly right, the leather mellowed, the gilt rubbed at exactly the places a thumb would rub it. She opened the cover. The title leaf was right. She turned to the middle of the *Antigone* and held a single page up against the flame.
The paper was wrong.

It was good paper. It was laid, and creamy, and pleasantly rough to the finger. But the chain lines stood a hair too far apart, and in the lower corner, where the light came through, there floated the pale ghost of a watermark. She brought her glass to it. It showed a small crowned shield with a letter beneath, and Aldus Manutius of Venice had never in his life printed on a sheet that bore it.
Harriet lowered the book. Her pulse had quickened, as it did when a sum would not come out.

*Sophocles, Aldine, 8vo,* she wrote. *Binding apparently of the period. Paper not. Watermark a stranger’s.* She underlined the last word, since it pleased her, and was reaching for the next volume on the shelf when the terrace doors at her back burst open.

The storm came in first. A blast of snow swept the length of the carpet, the lamps leaped, and two of her loose sheets took wing toward the fire. Then a man came in after it, stamping, and shouldered the doors shut with a crash that rattled the glass cases.

He was very tall. That was her first impression, and her second was of darkness, a long battered greatcoat white to the capes, black hair hanging wet to his collar, a jaw that had not met a razor in a week. He carried a lantern. He stripped off his hat, beat it against his thigh, and only then appeared to notice that the library was occupied.
He went perfectly still. His gaze traveled from the gold silk to the open notebook to the red morocco octavo in her hand, and it stopped there.
“Put that down,” he said.
“I beg your pardon?”

“The Aldine Sophocles. You are holding it by the boards, with a lamp six inches from the text block. Put it down flat, if you please, and tell me who the devil you are and what you are doing to my books.”
He had not come near enough to read the label on the shelf. Harriet noted that fact, and set it aside.
“Your books, sir?”
A pause followed, brief as a blink.

“The duke’s books. I have the charge of the estate, and they stand upon it.” He came forward into the lamplight, leaving wet prints on the carpet. Seen closer he was perhaps two-and-thirty, with a thin white scar running along the line of his jaw under the stubble, and a pair of very dark eyes that did not appear to miss much. “Graves. Land steward, for the present. I was hired from London in November to look into the drains.”

“Harriet Lisle. I was hired from Oxford in December to look into the library. I hold a signed engagement from Mr. Finch to catalogue every volume in this room, and I was not informed that I required the consent of the drains.” She did not put the Sophocles down. “Do you commonly enter by the terrace, Mr. Graves, in a blizzard?”
“When I see a light in a room that ought to be dark, yes.”
“It ought to be dark so early?”

“It has been dark every evening since I came.” He set his lantern on the reading table, beside her notebook, and his eye fell upon the open page before she could turn it. She saw him read the entry. A muscle moved in his cheek. “So. You are quick, I will grant you. Are you paid by the page, Miss Lisle, or by the volume you fail to notice is missing?”
“I have been in this room two hours. I have not yet had leisure to fail at anything.”
“And in that time you have gone straight to the one book on that shelf worth stealing.”

“I went straight to the Greek. I read Greek. It is not yet a hanging matter.” She shut the notebook. “And since we are exchanging suspicions, sir, allow me mine. You knew this volume from the far end of a room forty paces long. You called it by its printer. You spoke of the boards and the text block. Does a land steward usually know Venetian laid paper from a modern imitation?”
“I did not say a word about paper.”
“You read it in my notes, and you were not surprised.”
He was silent. The snow hissed against the tall windows, and a drop of meltwater ran from his hair down the scar and into his collar.
“Perhaps I am a very literate brute,” he said at last.
“Perhaps you are a very badly disguised one.”

It was a rash thing to say to a stranger twice her size in an empty wing of a snowbound house, and she regretted it as it left her lips. Mr. Graves did not appear to take offense. He looked, for one unguarded instant, as though he would have liked to laugh.
“As what, pray?”
“I have not determined. I form no opinion of any person until I have evidence.”
“You formed one of me before I had shut the door.”

“That was a hypothesis.” She held out the Sophocles to him across the table, spine first. “Here. Since you are so anxious for its safety, examine it yourself. Tell me what you see, and I shall tell you whether you are a steward.”
She had meant it as a challenge. She was not prepared for what he did with it.

He had kept his gloves on all this while, great stained leather gauntlets fit for mending a wall. He drew them off now, one finger at a time, and laid them on the table. The hands underneath were long and lean, and the first two fingers of the right were dyed to the second knuckle with old ink, the deep and settled stain of a man who had held a pen every day for twenty years.
He took the little book from her as a priest takes a chalice.

He did not open it at once. He turned it to the lamp, as she had done, and ran the ball of his thumb down the joint of the spine. He weighed it on his palm. Then he let it fall open, supporting the boards so that the binding should not strain, and bent his dark head over the page, and Harriet, watching, forgot to breathe out.

She had known men who loved books. Her father loved them. But she had seldom seen a pair of hands so exactly certain of where to hold and where to spare, and never on a person who claimed to have been hired for the drains.

“The morocco is old,” he said, low, as if to himself. “It is the true cover. Some other book was cut out of it, and this sewn in. See here, at the hinge, the new thread. And the paper.” He lifted a leaf against the flame. “Dutch, or made to pass for it. Thirty years old at the outside. The type has been cut to match, and cut well. This was no hackwork, Miss Lisle. A master did it.”
“So you do see it.”
“I have seen it since November. I could not prove it. I had not your eye for a watermark.” He raised his head. “How many have you found?”
“One. I told you, I have had two hours.”
“There will be others. I would stake the roof on it.”
“And the true Sophocles?”
“Gone.” He closed the forgery very gently. “Sold, I suppose, to some collector who asked no questions, and this pretty changeling left in its cradle so that nobody should miss it.”
“By whom?”
“If I could tell you that, I should not be coming in at windows.”
They had both reached to return the book to its place. Her hand closed on the spine at the same instant as his, and his bare ink-stained fingers lay across her knuckles, cold from the storm.

Neither of them moved. Neither spoke. Harriet was conscious, with great clearness, of the grain of the old morocco under her palm and the exact weight of each of his fingers upon hers, and of a slow heat that climbed from her wrist to her throat and had no business in a scholarly inquiry. His eyes had dropped to their joined hands. He seemed to be reading them as he had read the page.
The supper bell rang in the passage.

“Miss Lisle! Mr. Graves, if that is you tracking snow over my carpet!” Mrs. Mabbott’s voice carried through the door like a dinner gong. “There is a hot fowl on the table in the small parlor, and Mr. Finch is waiting to carve.”
He took his hand away. She slid the Sophocles into its gap on the shelf and found that her fingers were not altogether obedient.

“A moment,” Mr. Graves said, as she gathered her notebooks. He had picked up his gauntlets and was pulling them on again, covering the ink. “I have a favor to ask. I had sooner it were an order, but I perceive you do not take them.”
“What is it?”
“Say nothing of this at supper. The watermark, the hinge, any of it. Above all, say nothing to Finch.”
“Mr. Finch is my employer, sir. He signed my engagement. If the duke’s library has been robbed, he is the first person who ought to be told.”
“He is the last.”
“On what grounds?”
“I have none I can show you tonight.”

“Then you are asking me to conceal a theft from the duke’s own secretary, on the bare word of a stranger who came in by the terrace and will not account for his fingers.” Harriet tucked the notebooks under her arm. “I regret to disoblige you, Mr. Graves. I have a rooted objection to bare words. I do not take them, and I do not give them. I shall promise you nothing.”
“Not even your silence?”
“That least of all.”
He inclined his head. She had expected anger, and what she saw in the unshaven face was nearer to a rueful sort of respect.
“Then I must take my chance,” he said, and held the door for her.

Mr. Finch was all solicitude at supper. He carved the fowl with a flourish and inquired how she had found the library, and whether the lamps were sufficient, and whether she had yet come upon anything of interest among the classics. Across the table the land steward ate in silence, in his shirtsleeves, with his eyes on his plate.
Harriet opened her mouth to answer.
“I have barely begun, sir,” she heard herself say. “I have counted the bays and admired the ceiling. I shall have more to tell you in a week.”

She had promised nothing. She was entirely free to mention the Sophocles over the pudding, and she assured herself of it twice more before the cloth was drawn, and went up to bed without having said a word.
