paras: *Christmas Day, 1815*
“You will be betrothed by Twelfth Night, Felix, or I leave every farthing to Reginald.”

The Dowager Marchioness of Stratton delivered this sentence from a high-backed chair beside the library fire, in black velvet and a great many diamonds, on Christmas morning, directly after church. She did not raise her voice. She had not needed to raise it since the old king was a young man.
From the window seat at the far end of the room, half hidden by a curtain, Miss Judith Carrow observed the effect upon the gentleman addressed.

It was slight. The Marquess of Stratton stood on the hearthrug with his shoulders against the mantel and both hands thrust deep in his pockets, a long, lean, dark young man with a mouth that seemed permanently on the edge of amusement. He had come in from church with snow on his boots. He heard his grandmother out as another man might have heard the price of oats, and then he laughed.
“Reginald! Grandmama, you would never do it. You cannot abide him. He has hands like a pair of wet fish, and he addresses his own horse as ‘Sir.’”

“He is a Danvers, he is thirty, and he would marry a hatstand if I pointed at one. You are nine-and-twenty. You have had three excellent young women in this house in as many winters, with their mothers and their trunks, and each of them went home in a fortnight without an offer.”
“They were charming girls. I wished them every happiness.”
“Miss Fanshawe wept in the carriage.”
“Miss Fanshawe wept at breakfast when the eggs were hard. I did not feel I could take the credit.”

“Do not be flippant with me, sir. I am eighty-one years old, and I do not mean to die and leave this house to a man who thinks a joke is the same thing as a character.” The cane tapped once upon the carpet. “I have asked a party for the twelve days. They arrive the day after tomorrow, snow permitting. Lady Vane brings her daughter. Among them you will find a suitable wife, and you will court her like a gentleman instead of a performing ape. My Twelfth Night Ball is on the fifth. You will give me a name before the cake is cut.”
“And if I do not?”
“Then Reginald may count the spoons.”

A lesser man would have blustered. Lord Stratton merely tipped his head on one side, and a look moved for an instant behind the lazy dark eyes that was neither lazy nor amused. It was gone before Judith could name it.
“Twelve days,” he said. “You are a great believer in my powers, ma’am. I could not get Miss Fanshawe to pass the salt in fourteen.”
“I am no believer in them whatever. That is why I have engaged assistance.” The Dowager turned her head. “Miss Carrow, you may come forward. You have seen the worst of him now.”
Judith rose from the window seat.

She had arrived the previous evening, in the dark, by the last chaise to cross the river before the snow closed the road, and had been shown directly to her room. She had dressed this morning as she dressed for every first engagement. Her gown was burgundy wool, cut close and plain and buttoned to the throat, and no pupil of hers had ever seen a crease in it. Her dark curls were pinned back as firmly as curls could be. In her right hand she carried a small book bound in black cloth, and a pencil.
The marquess straightened from the mantel by a fraction of an inch. His glance went over her, quick and thorough, from the pins to the pencil, and his eyebrows rose.
“Good Lord,” he said. “Grandmama, you have brought in a chaperon for the heiresses before there are any heiresses. Is she to sit in a corner and count how often I smile?”
“Miss Carrow has not come to mind the young ladies, Felix. She has come to mind you.”
“I beg your pardon?”
“She is here as your tutor.”

There was a pause. It was a brief one, but Judith had spent seven years studying the faces of pupils who had just been told they were to be improved, and she took a private and unprofessional pleasure in this one.
“You have hired me a governess,” said Lord Stratton.

“I have hired you *the* governess. Miss Carrow finished Lady Sophia Marchant, who had a stammer and a squint and is now a countess. She finished both the Ponsonby girls. She took the Wetherby heiress in hand, who had been expelled from two seminaries for biting, and married her to a bishop’s nephew in a single Season.” The old lady folded her hands on the head of her cane. “She is the most expensive creature of her kind in England. She has never failed.”
“Has she not?” He turned the full force of a very charming smile upon the black cloth book. “Then I shall enjoy being her first.”
“I doubt it, my lord,” Judith said.
It was the first time he had heard her voice. It was a low one, and exceedingly clear, and it had been known to stop a schoolroom riot at forty paces.
“Do you? On what grounds?”

“Pupils who set out to fail me commonly find that it requires more effort than passing. I have not yet met one who could keep it up for twelve days.” She curtsied to the Dowager, to the correct depth and no deeper. “With your leave, ma’am, I shall begin in an hour. I should like to see his lordship walk down a staircase.”
“You wish to watch me descend?” said the marquess.
“A gentleman reveals a good deal upon a staircase. The grand one, if you please. In one hour precisely.”

She went out with her book under her arm. Behind her she heard the Dowager give a short crack of laughter, and a pleasant, incredulous voice inquiring whether biting was to be permitted on both sides.
He was late, as she had been certain he would be.

The grand staircase of Stratton Park swept down into the great hall in a double curve of white marble, and Mrs. Pell, the housekeeper, had dressed it for Christmas with garlands of pine tied up in scarlet ribbon. A ball of mistletoe hung over the first landing. Judith had taken her position upon the main flight at five minutes before the hour, with the clock in view, and she had now been standing there for a quarter of an hour by its hands.

He did not come down the staircase at all. He strolled in from the direction of the stables, by a side door, with a spaniel at his heels, and arranged himself against the newel post at the foot as if it had been put there for the purpose. His hands were in his pockets. He was smirking.

Judith did not descend to him. She stopped three steps above, where her eyes were a full foot higher than his, and folded her arms. Her first year had taught her that a governess ought never to surrender the high ground.
“You are late, my lord. And your hands are in your pockets.”

“It is December, Miss Carrow. My hands are cold.” He looked up at her through his lashes, in a manner that had doubtless been found devastating in a number of London ballrooms. “Though if you are offering to warm them, I am famously open to unconventional teaching.”

“I am offering to save your inheritance from a man who calls his own horse ‘Sir.’ Hands out. Stand up straight.” She waited. He did neither. “And stop regarding me as though I were a particularly amusing spaniel.”

“I would never insult a spaniel so. Spaniels are eager to please.” The dog at his feet thumped its tail in confirmation. “You, I suspect, prefer to bite. Is that where the Wetherby girl acquired the habit, or did you cure her of it by example?”
“I cured her of it by declining to be interesting to bite. She found she preferred conversation. You may find the same.”
“I converse beautifully. Ask anybody.”

“I have asked. I have made inquiries about you for a fortnight, my lord, since your grandmother first wrote.” She opened the black book. “You talk a great deal and say nothing. You have danced with every heiress in London and offended half of them by laughing in the middle of the set. You told Lady Jersey at her own table that matrimony was an excellent institution for people who liked institutions. You leave town in the middle of every Season, without explanation, and nobody can discover where you go.”
For the second time that morning a shadow stirred in the dark eyes and was instantly put away.
“I go to Yorkshire,” he said lightly. “I have a grandmother in it. She is very exacting.”
“So I have observed.”
“And what is your prescription, ma’am? Backboard? Bread and water? Am I to write out ‘I must not laugh at heiresses’ a hundred times?”

“Twelve lessons. One for each day. Tomorrow you will learn to listen to a lady without flirting with her. After that we shall take dancing, and conduct at table, and how to walk out, and a number of other matters you believe you already know. On the eleventh day you will learn to make a proposal of marriage without a single joke in it.”
“Twelve days.” He shook his head in mock sorrow. “God made the world in six. Surely you do not need twelve to make me tolerable.”
“God began with light and firmament, my lord. I am beginning with an overgrown rake who thinks mocking a country dance counts as wit.”

He laughed. It broke out of him before he could prevent it, a quick warm shout that rang up the marble well and startled the spaniel, and for a moment the smirk was replaced by an entirely different expression. It was surprise. He looked like a fencer who has been touched in the first exchange by a schoolgirl.
Judith noted it. She noted also that he had a remarkably pleasant laugh, and that the fact was of no professional relevance, and she wrote neither thing down.
“I have been called a good many things on that staircase, chiefly by my grandmother,” he said. “Never that. I begin to think you may be worth your fee.”
“I am worth a good deal more than my fee. Your hands are still in your pockets.”
“So they are.” He glanced down at them with mild interest. “They appear to like it there.”

“A gentleman who courts a lady with his hands in his pockets tells her that he is holding himself in reserve. That he has not troubled to bring all of himself to the conversation. It is the habit of a man who does not intend to be caught caring about anything.”
She had said it as she would have said it to any pupil, crisply, as a point of deportment. She was not prepared for the result.

The amusement went out of his face. It did not vanish. It was withdrawn, like a hand from a fire, and for the space of a breath the Marquess of Stratton stood at the foot of his own staircase with no expression at all, looking up at her, and she had the sudden uncomfortable sense of having put her pencil through a painted screen and struck a wall behind it.
Then the smile came back, easier than ever.
“You have me exactly,” he said. “I care for nothing whatever, Miss Carrow. I should not know how to begin. It is the secret of my complexion.”
“Then you will not mind losing a fortune to your cousin.”
“Not in the least.”
“You argued the point with some energy for a man who does not mind.”

“I dislike Reginald. It is not the same thing as liking money.” He took one hand from its pocket at last, but only to scratch the spaniel’s ears. “I will tell you what I do mind, since we are to be so frank. I mind being managed. My grandmother has managed this county for sixty years, and I am the last thing in it that will not go where she points. I mean to keep the distinction. So I will make you a wager.”
“I do not wager with pupils.”

“A small one. I bet you that I shall be the first you ever fail. Twelve days, twelve lessons, and on Twelfth Night I shall be precisely as unbetrothed and as ill-behaved as you see me now. If I win, you tell my grandmother to her face that I am past mending, and she leaves me in peace for a twelvemonth.”
“And if I win?”
“You will not.”
“If I win, my lord.”
He considered her, with his head on one side. The spaniel leaned against his boot.
“If you win, I shall take my hands out of my pockets for the rest of my natural life,” said Lord Stratton, “and you may have it in writing.”

She ought to have refused. A governess of her standing did not bet. It was undignified, and it placed the instructress on a level with the instructed, and she had told a dozen headstrong heiresses that she was not to be drawn into contests of will.
“Done,” said Judith.
The word was out before she had weighed it. She shut her mouth, a good deal annoyed, and he grinned up at her in open delight, as though she had passed some examination of his own.
“Tomorrow, then, Miss Carrow, after breakfast. Where am I to be improved?”
“The music room. You will be punctual.”
“I shall be magnificent,” he promised, and sauntered away across the hall with the dog trotting after, whistling a carol, both hands returned to his pockets before he reached the door.
Judith remained upon the third step. She found that her arms were still folded, a great deal more tightly than deportment required, and she unfolded them.

She had come to Stratton Park to perform a piece of work. It was her trade. Marriage, as she had explained to forty anxious mothers, was a sensible merger between suitable parties, and her task was to see that the parties presented well and that nobody’s feelings were permitted to spoil a sound arrangement. She had done it for dukes’ daughters. She saw no reason why it could not be done for one idle marquess, with a pleasant laugh and a wall behind his eyes.
She opened the black cloth book to a fresh page. At the head of it, in her small exact hand, she wrote *Stratton.*
She considered it. Then, for the first time in seven years of teaching, Miss Carrow drew a line beneath a pupil’s name, and after a moment’s further thought, drew a second.
